newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British unemployment - great figure, but lacks weight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British unemployment - great figure, but lacks weight.

text.p: Britain's official unemployment statistics make for an impressive first read.
Unemployment has fallen for 16 months in succession, hitting a new six year low of 6.2 percent of the workforce in February.
The unemployment rate is fast approaching 6.0 percent, unrivalled by Europe's major economies, and the jobless total has fallen by a third since the Conservatives won the last election in 1992.
But scratch the surface and cracks soon start to appear.

Five years of economic growth have yielded only a tiny increase in employment. Job creation is patchy, has fallen far short of expectations and is growing well below the rate the huge monthly falls in unemployment suggest.
And with the May 1 election only weeks away, British voters appear sceptical about the rosy picture painted by the official data.

Leading pollster MORI found that despite the steady fall in the statistics, unemployment is the issue voters rate as the third most important facing Britain today after education and health. Among the youngest voters, it comes second only to education.
This suggests the public's experience of unemployment differs widely from official perceptions.

"The fact that it is still so high on the list suggests the reality people are facing is rather different to what the official figures show," said Cara Lavan, reasearch executive at MORI. "If unemployment were really falling as fast as the figures say, the issue should be further down the list."

The opposition Labour Party says the official figures, which measure the number of people allowed to claim unemployment benefit rather than those who would like a job but cannot find one, are wildly inaccurate.
Labour's employment spokesman David Blunkett called the February data "fantasy figures" and said they had been fiddled.
"What we do know is that one in five households have no-one in work. Since John Major became Prime Minister we have lost one million jobs," he said.
FIGURES MASK REALITY
Even the government, keen to trumpet its economic successes before the election, has been embarrassed into admitting the data exaggerate its employment record.
Early in the election campaign, the usually irrepressible Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine confessed that only about half of the monthly falls were due to job creation.
"Something like half the reduction that we're seeing is through new jobs," he said after official figures showed a huge 68,200 fall in February.
The other half of recent monthly falls comes from the latest change to the calculation of the claimant count.
In October, the government scrapped unemployment benefit and replaced it with a new "Jobs Seekers' Allowance," which brought with it more rigorous eligibility criteria.
This followed around 30 other changes in the way unemployment is calculated since the Conservatives took office in 1979.
Britain is now unique in defining unemployment as people eligible for benefit and able to prove they are activity seeking work.
The Employment Policy Institute, a leading independent research group, says the Conservatives' record on jobs is at best mixed.
"The Conservatives have been very good at getting people off the claimant count, but less successful at getting them into jobs," said Nick Isles, the institute's director of development.

Another independent report from Sheffield Hallam University calculated that in January, unemployment was really more than double the official 1.8 million rate of because large numbers of jobless people are "hidden" from government figures.
The difference was accounted for by unemployed people ineligible for benefits, those on government schemes or long-term jobless hidden among those regarded as early retired or permanently sick.
The researchers said 1.2 million long-term unemployed were excluded from the official monthly figures, while the number of long-term sick people of working age had tripled in the past 15 years.

Some statisticians have lost patience with the quality of the data, especially since plans to produce monthly data using internationally recognised methodology were shelved last year due to funding constraints.

"The claimant count is not trusted, is not based on any agreed concept of unemployment, is inconsistent over time due to changes in the claimant system and cannot be used for international comparisons," the Royal Statistical Society said.
OTHER FIGURES PAINT A BLEAKER PICTURE
The internationally approved calculations used in the government's own quarterly Labour Force Survey paint a less remarkable picture of the British jobs market.
In the three months to November last year, unemployment as recorded by the Labour Force Survey fell by just 32,000 -- dramatically less that the 114,000 drop seen in claimant unemployment.

Since 1992, employment has grown by just 388,000 in a workforce of around 25 million, according to the Survey. This is in sharp contrast to the monthly official figures which show unemployment down by 771,400 to stand at 1,815,300 in January.

The quality of the new jobs that have been created has also been questioned. "Of the new jobs created since 1992, two-thirds are part-time, and of the full-time jobs, around half are temporary," said Isles.
In its manifesto, the Conservative party has promised more of the same.

Vowing to stay out of the European Union's Social Chapter, which sets out rights for workers, it says its priority is to create jobs through continued deregulation, cutting red tape and attracting investment from overseas.

Labour plans to spend three billion pounds ($4.9 billion) on creating 250,000 jobs for young people and the long-term unemployed, financed from a one-off windfall tax on the profits of privatised utility companies.
But given its commitment to tight public spending, Labour may find it difficult to finance an effective programme.
"There is no such thing as a free lunch when it comes to these schemes," Isles said. "Three billion pounds is just about enough to get a scheme started, but to sustain it may require a bit extra."
($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
